fields.definition: In the OAIS reference model (ISO 14721), the information package an archive assembles from one or more Archival Information Packages (AIPs) and delivers to a Consumer in response to an order or request. A DIP contains the requested content plus Packaging Information, and may carry full or partial Preservation Description Information, formatted for access, exchange, or system transfer rather than for long-term storage.
fields.plain_english: It is the copy an archive hands out when someone asks for a recording. The archive builds it from its stored master, then shapes it for easy use rather than for long storage.
fields.purpose_function: It separates what an archive gives out from what it keeps, so the preserved master (the AIP) stays untouched while users receive a version tailored for access, sharing, or migration to another system.
fields.practical_application: An audio archivist generates a DIP, such as an access-quality WAV or MP3 plus a metadata sheet, when a researcher, broadcaster, or partner institution requests material from the preservation store.
common_mistakes: Confusing the DIP with the AIP; the AIP is the preserved master, while the DIP is the delivery copy derived from it
Assuming a DIP must contain the whole archival package, when it often carries only the part a consumer ordered plus packaging information
Treating a DIP as a preservation copy and discarding the AIP after exporting it
scenario_contexts: Exporting an access-quality file and metadata for a researcher who requested a specific recording
Packaging content with complete metadata to hand a collection to another institution
Preparing a standardized DIP to transfer holdings to a successor archive system

sources: ISO 14721 / CCSDS 650.0-M-2, Reference Model for an Open Archival Information System (OAIS)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects, sec. 6.1.8 (OAIS)
Digital Preservation Coalition, OAIS wiki: Types of Information Packages

fields.definition: The process of confirming that a digital audio file or bitstream has remained unchanged, or fixed, over time or through transfer, typically by generating a checksum or cryptographic hash and comparing it against a previously stored reference value. A mismatch indicates corruption, alteration, or an incomplete transfer.
fields.plain_english: It is a way to prove a file has not changed. The computer makes a short code from the file, then later makes the code again and checks that the two still match.
fields.purpose_function: It gives an archive proof that stored files stay bit-for-bit identical, detecting silent data corruption, failed transfers, or tampering so a damaged file can be replaced from a good copy.
fields.practical_application: Preservation systems compute checksums at ingest and at scheduled intervals, flagging any file whose hash no longer matches its recorded value so it can be repaired from a redundant copy.
common_mistakes: Believing fixity verification repairs files; it only detects change, and repair requires a known-good redundant copy
Recording a checksum once at ingest but never re-checking, so slow corruption goes unnoticed
Assuming a matching checksum proves audio quality, when it only proves the bits are unchanged, not that the original transfer was good
scenario_contexts: Verifying that a file transferred to archival storage matches the checksum recorded at ingest
Running scheduled integrity sweeps across a repository to catch bit rot on aging media
Confirming a retrieved file is intact before delivering it to a user

sources: Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook: Fixity and checksums
NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (File Fixity and Data Integrity)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects, sec. 6.3 (Archival Storage / verification)

fields.definition: The proactive practice of monitoring the file and encoding formats held in an archive for signs of obsolescence, such as loss of software or hardware support and backward compatibility, and planning timely migration to sustainable, well-documented formats before the content becomes inaccessible.
fields.plain_english: It means watching the file types you store and getting ready before they stop working. Old formats can become unreadable, so you plan to move the content into newer formats in good time.
fields.purpose_function: It protects long-term access by making sure files are never trapped in a format that current software can no longer open, guiding both format choice and migration timing.
fields.practical_application: Archivists track format risk using registries such as PRONOM, prefer open lossless formats like WAV and BWF for masters, and schedule migration when a format's support begins to decline.
common_mistakes: Storing masters in proprietary or lossy formats that raise obsolescence risk instead of open, lossless, well-documented ones
Waiting until a format is already unreadable to act, rather than planning migration in advance
Assuming an open format can never become obsolete, when adoption and tool support still have to be monitored
scenario_contexts: Reviewing collection formats against a format-risk registry during an annual audit
Deciding to migrate a legacy encoded collection while conversion tools still exist
Selecting a sustainable master format when setting up a new digitization workflow

sources: Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook: File formats and standards
IASA-TC 03, The Safeguarding of the Audiovisual Heritage, sec. 4 (Obsolescence of formats)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (target formats / preservation planning)

fields.definition: A storage strategy in which complete copies of archived content are kept at two or more physically separate locations, ideally in areas subject to different disaster threats, so that a localized event such as fire, flood, or power loss cannot destroy every copy.
fields.plain_english: It means keeping copies of your files in different places that are far apart. If one site is hit by a fire or flood, the copies stored somewhere else still survive.
fields.purpose_function: It hedges against regional and site-level threats by ensuring no single physical event can take out all copies, a requirement built into preservation frameworks such as the NDSA Levels.
fields.practical_application: An archive keeps one copy on-site and additional copies in data centers in other regions, or on offline media held elsewhere, so recovery is still possible after a local disaster.
common_mistakes: Keeping all copies in the same building or region, which gives no protection against a local disaster
Counting copies without checking they sit in locations with genuinely different disaster threats
Assuming a cloud provider gives geographic redundancy by default without confirming where the copies physically reside
scenario_contexts: Placing a second copy of a master collection in a data center in a different region
Designing storage to meet a preservation level that requires copies in areas with different disaster threats
Recovering holdings from a remote copy after a flood damages the primary facility

sources: NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (Storage and Geographic Location)
Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook (storage / preservation)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (multiple storage locations)

fields.definition: The practice of safeguarding audio recordings of cultural, historical, or documentary significance for the long term, prioritizing the preservation of their content, meaning the signal and its associated information, over the original carrier, since analog and physical carriers inevitably deteriorate and become obsolete.
fields.plain_english: It is the work of saving important old recordings so future people can still hear them. Because tapes and discs wear out, the goal is to save the sound itself, not just the object it came on.
fields.purpose_function: It ensures that culturally valuable sound, such as music, oral history, broadcast, and field recordings, survives carrier decay and format change so the recorded content stays accessible for future generations.
fields.practical_application: Archivists appraise and prioritize significant collections, transfer at-risk carriers to digital preservation formats, and then manage the results under standards such as IASA-TC 03 and TC-04.
common_mistakes: Focusing on preserving the physical carrier while neglecting to transfer the content before the carrier fails
Treating a single digital transfer as permanent, ignoring the ongoing migration and integrity checking preservation requires
Making lossy or low-resolution transfers of irreplaceable material to save space, which degrades the archival master
scenario_contexts: Digitizing a deteriorating collection of magnetic tapes holding unique oral histories
Prioritizing which at-risk heritage recordings to transfer first based on significance and carrier condition
Maintaining and periodically migrating a digitized heritage collection to keep it accessible

sources: IASA-TC 03, The Safeguarding of the Audiovisual Heritage: Ethics, Principles and Preservation Strategy
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects
UNESCO Memory of the World Programme, guidance on audiovisual heritage preservation

fields.definition: The ongoing, scheduled recomputation and comparison of file checksums across the full lifetime of an archive, used to confirm that stored audio files remain bit-for-bit unchanged over years or decades and to detect gradual data corruption, or bit rot, as storage media age.
fields.plain_english: It means checking a file's fingerprint code again and again over many years. Doing it on a regular schedule catches slow damage before a file quietly rots away.
fields.purpose_function: It shifts trust away from the durability of any single storage medium toward repeated verification, so silent corruption is caught early and affected files repaired from a good copy.
fields.practical_application: Preservation systems store reference checksums and re-verify content at fixed intervals, often yearly for tape and more frequently for disk, logging the results and triggering repair when a hash fails.
common_mistakes: Calculating a checksum only at ingest and never revalidating, so long-term corruption goes undetected
Validating checksums but keeping no redundant copy to repair from when a file fails
Assuming newer storage media never degrade, so scheduled revalidation is skipped
scenario_contexts: Running an annual integrity sweep over an entire tape-based archive
Comparing current file hashes against reference values during a storage-system migration
Detecting and repairing a corrupted master file from a redundant copy after a failed check

sources: Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook: Fixity and checksums
NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (File Fixity and Data Integrity)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects, sec. 6.3 (Archival Storage / verification)

fields.definition: A documented archival policy defining when and how digital content is copied from aging or obsolescent storage media and systems onto current ones, along with the verification required, in order to counter the limited lifespan and obsolescence of storage carriers and hardware.
fields.plain_english: It is a written plan for moving files onto fresh storage before the old storage fails. Since drives and tapes do not last forever, the plan says when to move data and how to check it copied correctly.
fields.purpose_function: It ensures content outlives any single storage medium or system by scheduling regular transfers to current media, with fixity checks so nothing is lost or corrupted during the move.
fields.practical_application: An archive follows its policy to refresh or migrate collections onto new LTO tape generations or storage systems on a set cycle, verifying checksums before retiring the old media.
common_mistakes: Confusing media migration, which moves bits to new storage, with format migration, which changes the file format
Migrating data without verifying checksums, so existing corruption is copied forward undetected
Delaying migration until the media are already failing or the reading hardware is obsolete
scenario_contexts: Copying a collection onto a new LTO tape generation before the old drives are unsupported
Scheduling routine storage-refresh cycles as part of a preservation plan
Verifying fixity on both source and destination during a system migration

sources: IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects, sec. 6.3-6.4 (Archival Storage / Digital Preservation Planning)
Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook: Preservation action
NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (Storage / ongoing management)

fields.definition: A preservation strategy of maintaining several complete, independent copies of archived content, typically three or more on different storage systems and often in different locations, so that the failure, loss, or corruption of any one copy does not endanger the content.
fields.plain_english: It means keeping more than one full copy of everything you store. If one copy is lost or damaged, another good copy is still there to restore from.
fields.purpose_function: It removes reliance on any single copy or device, because redundant copies let a corrupted or destroyed file be rebuilt from an intact one and underpin fixity-based repair.
fields.practical_application: Archives keep a primary copy plus independent backups on separate systems and sites, following guidance such as the NDSA Levels or the 3-2-1 rule, and repair failed files from a healthy copy.
common_mistakes: Keeping several copies on the same drive or system, which share a single point of failure
Assuming a RAID array counts as multiple copies, when RAID is not a backup or an independent copy
Never verifying the copies, so all of them may already be corrupt when one is finally needed
scenario_contexts: Storing three independent copies of a master collection across different systems
Rebuilding a corrupted file from a redundant copy after a failed fixity check
Applying the 3-2-1 backup rule when designing archival storage

sources: NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (Storage and Geographic Location)
Digital Preservation Coalition, Digital Preservation Handbook (storage / multiple copies)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (redundant copies)

fields.definition: A digital archive whose design and operations conform to the Open Archival Information System (OAIS) reference model (ISO 14721 / CCSDS 650.0), implementing its functional entities, namely Ingest, Archival Storage, Data Management, Administration, Preservation Planning, and Access, together with its information-package model of SIP, AIP, and DIP, to preserve digital content and keep it accessible to a designated community over the long term.
fields.plain_english: It is an archive built to follow one shared set of rules for keeping digital files safe and usable for a long time. Using the same rules lets different archives work alike and share files.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a common framework and vocabulary so long-term preservation is systematic and interoperable, ensuring content is ingested, stored, managed, and delivered with the metadata needed to stay understandable over time.
fields.practical_application: Audio archives adopt the OAIS model to structure their systems and workflows, taking content in as SIPs, preserving it as AIPs, and delivering DIPs to users.
common_mistakes: Thinking OAIS is a piece of software or a certification, rather than a reference model that systems are designed to conform to
Implementing storage only and ignoring OAIS functions such as Preservation Planning and Data Management
Confusing OAIS conformance with trustworthy-repository certification, such as ISO 16363, which is a separate audit
scenario_contexts: Designing a new audio preservation repository around the six OAIS functional entities
Mapping ingest and delivery workflows to the SIP, AIP, and DIP model
Assessing whether an existing archive meets the OAIS mandatory responsibilities

sources: ISO 14721 / CCSDS 650.0-M-2, Reference Model for an Open Archival Information System (OAIS)
IASA-TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects, sec. 6.1.8 (OAIS)
Digital Preservation Coalition, technology watch report: The Open Archival Information System (OAIS) Reference Model
